reviews.text: Force feeding a raven a coin is my new favourite hobby.

EDIT: The latest patch is *chef’s kiss.* Literally everything that a Steam friend and I both requested via Discord (and notes in our reviews) has been addressed within the last nine days or so since release from what I can see. Controller support is smooth, new card scrolling and highlighting is perfect for drawing attention to each card, gameplay tips emerge on screen as you scroll cards, and there’s a toggle-able static key bindings list on screen so you know exactly what buttons do what. Stellar update. Dawncaster feels made for Deck now. I am not surprised, given these devs track record, but I’m so so happy and appreciative! BRAVO!!! Truly the best devs I’ve ever seen in my life. This is one of the only games I have on my iPhone. I bought Dawncaster back when it was a hidden gem, and watched it steadily climb the charts to now currently sit at the #7 card game in the App Store! Hands-down, the Dawncaster developers are THE GOLD STANDARD in my book. They are the most passionate, responsive, kind guys. They’re constantly in the Discord responding immediately to players who have any sort of question or suggestion. I own thousands of games across multiple platforms and have been a lifelong gamer and the Dawncaster devs are the standard by which I compare ALL other game devs. As for the game itself, I have many many hours in it on iPhone, and I bought each expansion as it released. Here on Steam they have released all of the expansions bundled with the base game for an incredibly generous price. Dawncaster is loaded with content. The base game is massive, and each expansion has been stuffed to the brim with content. (Note that any DLC with “Support” in the title is cosmetic only, and affects the gameplay in no way at all, only changes card art). The gameplay is really fun. They’ve blended genuine RPG gameplay with deckbuilding in a compelling way. The RPG elements give you a unique sense of immersion and ownership. There are over a thousand unique cards, soooo many buffs and debuffs, and a wide variety of characters//classes to play, with diverse character artwork from which to choose. As you progress through the game, you earn the ability to unlock more classes, skins, weapons cards, etc. The replayability is truly endless. I’m someone who is easily overwhelmed by deckbuilding mechanics, and often a bit “shy” about trying new deckbuilders. But with Dawncaster, the devs have done a marvelous job of making the early game quite approachable (with a great tutorial, and a number of difficulty features you can toggle on and off). Feeling “competent” in this game sooner rather than later hooked me instantly. And for experienced deckbuilder people, Dawncaster has tons of content, and you can skip tutorials. The devs have managed to make this game something special for all skill and experience levels. I instantly bought this again on Steam both to support the devs, but also to have this for my Deck and Legion Go. (Be sure to force use of either Proton Experimental or Proton 9.0 or newer or else the game won’t boot.) I’ve been testing it out in handheld and it’s running pretty great. I’ve fiddled with some runs and am really impressed with the translation from iPhone to Steam. The vibrant artwork looks spectacular on a bigger screen. Controller support works for most things, though I have had to use the touchscreen for some items. I’ve spotted a few bugs here and there (cards popping up in your hand when they shouldn’t, a boss remaining static on screen blocking card selection, a soft-lock after a boss turn where I didn’t have an option to continue with my turn), and have some suggestions for improvements (state on screen which buttons do what, such as “X” to inspect cards, “A” to play cards; make selections more obvious on screen via highlights or enlarging objects). I mentioned any and all bugs and suggestions in Discord and the devs IMMEDIATELY responded to each one. Like, literally within seconds. If you encounter any bugs I will tell you this: You can 100% trust these devs to polish and perfect this game on Steam. I do not know these guys; I’ve mostly been a Discord lurker. But I have seen them respond instantly to everyone on Discord over the years, and then today they did the same with me, despite me being a virtual stranger in their Discord, with promises to quickly patch for little bugs I found or bigger suggestions I have! You can trust these guys. They communicate everything with their players upfront and they speedily deliver what and when they promise. If you’re a deckbuilder fan, you must try Dawncaster. If you’re an RPG fan, even more reason!

I've played many (TOO MANY) deckbuilder games and for me, the RPG and storytelling is what sets this one apart. I was recommended this by a friend (you know who you are teehee ^_^) and was hesitant because it is a mobile port. But I am so happy I gave this game a chance because it doesn't play like a mobile game and offers so much for the pricetag, including all the expansions. If anything, I am 3 hours in and feeling overwhelemed with all the choices. There are an array of characters to pick from. You can pick your character portrait and starting weapon. You start with a limited pool but you can unlock more along the way, the weapons offerering different perks and supporting playstyles such as melee or ranged (which is so cool because when I think rogue, I think melee character. But there are starter weapons that are ranged under the rogue character playset). The possibilities seem endless for multiple playthroughs and I love how I am not pigeon holed in. You really can fully construct the character you want, albeit it may take some time and playthroughs to unlock the different cards, weapons etc. It really does feel like a role playing experience, as you have a story with objectives. You stop by towns to rest and interact with characters, There is a shopkeep and blacksmith. Just very well rounded and does indeed play like an RPG. You travel through the scenario and are given pathways to select from, similar to other deckbuilders out there. You collect cards and trinkets along the way to shape your character. My only comaplint is that the tutorial system is severly lacking. I was given the option to complete a tutorial after doing a couple runs when in reality, that scenario should be the FIRST one users are introducted to. Most of it is self explanatory if you have played a deckbuilder before, but if you are new you might be a bit lost. There are also little exclamation points on the lower left hand corner you can click on that offer pointers but I found that by chance. In addition, your cards in hand light up green or yellow. Green means that the card conditions are met (ie. you get the bonus on the card) where yellow means that you only get the most basic action on the card. This is never explained anywhere. Because this game is already out on mobile, you can find lots of resources online to help you out. But an integrated PROPER tutorial would be appreciated. An intro to the reward system and fateshards would also be helpful because I can see how that could be missed completely on the main page (that is where you unlock more character portraits, talents, starting cards etc). Overall, a really enjoyable deckbuilding experience if you are willing to be a bit more patient as you navigate it all. It really does have a lot to offer and unlock to make your runs feel individualistic, customizable and varied, with lots of scenarios and card options to fit every playstyle. Update: still enjoying the game but I got it for mobile and surprisingly, prefer playing it on there. It’s an uncomfortable play on the steam deck for me, controls are a bit wonky and aren’t really explained. Runs nice on PC tho. I’d actually recommend this game to be played on mobile for the best experience (oddly enough).

Controller support is atrocious. Multiple interactions are either cumbersome (many inputs for one action), unclear (poor highlighting) or straight up impossible on controller. The store claims full controller support. That's manifestly not true and the devs clearly know it. If it said "partial support" and will be patched after launch I'd have no issues, but intentionally misleading customers is an automatic negative review.

This game is a mobile port and you can really feel that. I play a lot of roguelite games, especially of the deckbuilding variety. This one wouldn't make my list, despite the tremendous amounts of cards and content. The main reason is the grindy, tedious nature of a mobile game. The way everything is balanced feels off. Usually being a veteran of this type of game pays off, as you can spot the synergies early on and make any kind of powerful build on the fly. Not here though. The actually viable options are behind endless grinding. Because the points you get even for an amazing run are capped. But the loop itself is far from interesting or satisfying enough to merit the grind. This is an exercise of wasting my time rather than a fun game. There is so much grinding, it's insane. And it's separate for every character. So not only am I expected to grind for weeks to unlock everything for 1 character, I literally have to stick to 1, because the rest of them are so far behind it's not even worth using them. This is why i hate mobile games. And the way the rewards are priced is so goofy. Why are the portraits so expensive? Why is there a once a day x2 bonus on points like a phone game? And the animations are so slow, you can skip or speed them up in any way. It adds so much to the tedium. Do not recommend buying at full price at all. 50% maybe. Or even better, buy Knocking on the Coffin lid. It's this game but 10 times better for the same price.

So after 12 hours and a few runs I have to not recommend this for people who like deckbuilders. There's good fun deckbuilding <here> in the game, but there's a couple of things that make me lean towards no. #1 The grind to unlock things is absolutely nonsense for a PC game. I presume this is from it's mobile origins, but my rough napkin maths suggests it'd take 600+ hours to unlock everything which would be fine if that was all cosmetic options etc, but it's not, it's deckbuilding options, it's the weapons, it's weapon powers etc are all in that big long list of stuff to unlock at glacial pace. #2 There are so many hard block "you lose because you are this type of deck" situations. For example, if you play the starter warrior deck and you roll the meadows as your starting location, if you fight the mole with the shield, you have lost. In the first location why? Because that deck ramps "on hit" and if the enemy has armour, you don't "hit", so you get blocked out from killing them. Playing the monk deck and fight "one"? good luck as he instantly bricks the combo part of your deck, then gains massive barrier each turn as you die from being unable to play cards out your hand because of their cost. Don't have a blessing dispel? Instantly lose to some places. Slow big attacks? Instantly lose to some places. It isn't fun, you don't feel like you've been outplayed, or you could have done better, you get to certain fights and it's the D&D equivalent of "rocks fall everyone dies", and because these are slower runs (1-2 hours to get towards the final boss) it feels real bad to lose to a "you instantly lost because you were on this route". #3 This one is less of a hard no than the other two for me, but it feels jank how the "recruited" system is a per run situation, it sucks that if you want enchantment imbues you <must> choose a certain area, I get it from a theming scenario, but from a gameplay scenario it means if you want X companion you must always choose Y route which is iffy for replayability.

Edit: As of Feb. 15th, 2026 a preliminary controller support rework was released. It has significantly improved controller, mouse, and keyboard support, but I'm still not comfortable saying that the game's PC inputs are in a good, recommendable state. I'll keep track of this as it changes and update this review accordingly. Original Review: This is a quick, cheap port of a phone game and it gets in the way enough to make the game border on being unplayable on a controller. They haven't even done the basic step of replacing text that says things like "tap with three fingers" with something appropriate for the input type you're using. There's barely any indication for which UI element is selected nor any indication for what any of the controller's buttons will do. Will "A" select a card to examine it or will "A" immediately play the card? You get to find out the hard way because the interface has not been updated in any noticeable way to support a controller. Just navigating the main menu to click the play button was a hassle. The underlying game could possibly be worth playing but it's not currently possible to evaluate that underlying game due to the huge pile of problems that should have been solved well before it was put up for sale with "full controller support" written on the store page. I don't know what, exactly, constitutes "full" controller support, but it's sure not this.

The fact that every single time I died felt like complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is the first reason I can't recommend this game. To illustrate, one run I was using a card that gives you barrier (blocks incoming damage, doesn't fade at the end of turn) and upgrades itself every time you play it, single use per combat. As I was steamrolling on everything, whatever enemy stole a random buff of mine and converted it entirely to burn (tick every end of turn), so I got 93 burn and died. Very cool. Every lost run looked more or less like that, if that's your thing go for it. There is also the fact that this game is extremely grindy, both in metaprogression and during the runs themselves. So far I have found no reason whatsoever to leave an area before having done all encounters available, as every fight gives you exp and leveling up grants you ridiculous talents with among them the traditional +1 mana every turn. Those encounters aren't unique, you'll keep fighting the same monsters over and over each area, it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ drag. That's how you get 2-3 hours runs. Balance is overall all over the place. Some trash mobs are somehow way more dangerous than the pushovers you get as final bosses, the cards' rarity doesn't mean ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and areas have NPC that are way too useful to ignore so you end up always going for the same stuff. Lastly, for a game that old I was expecting a polished UX/UI but even that was a disappointment, and I don't think that's due to it being a PC port. Behaviors are inconsistent, sometimes you got tooltips for the keywords, sometimes you don't, deck can only be displayed as a list on the side before picking an event choice, choices are clickable before they've rendered, etc. In other words I got baited once again. Oh yeah, there is exactly zero RPG element whatsoever in this game but I guess we should get used to every game being called an RPG for no reason these days.

I think it's a shame that Dawncaster is getting mixed reviews, as I think it is up there with the very best deckbuilders like Monster Train and Chrono Ark. The game has apparently been out on mobile for a long time, but it's new to me. Getting the bad out of the way first, the art is a little generic and not my favorite, and the story is disjointed gobbledygook. But I think this is *the* best deckbuilder in terms of content and build variety. The card pool is massive and varied, the passive talents you get on level-ups are exciting and actually contribute to your build (unlike the hodgepodge of stupid "relics" you end up with in Slay the Spire type games), and there are tons of enemies and areas. The interactions and synergies between the cards are great. Each of the 6 classes can pick from about 10 different weapons at the start of the run, and the weapon you pick will be the basic attacks in your deck (e.g. the starter cards that do 5 dmg that you replace as quick as you can). Except here, each weapon works very differently. For example, I mostly use the longbow hunter, and those "basic attacks" crit from ambush and give a stack of evade on crit. In other words, they would be a high-tier card in a different game. But the hunter could also use some serrated axes that inflict bleed instead. What Dawncaster does differently than any other deckbuilder that I know of is that some of the cards you can draft (but not all) interact with the "basic attack" mechanic. For example, there is a card called "Whirling Strikes" that will make a basic attack for every basic attack you've made that turn, and when it does that it plays the your starter weapon card over and over. So it could work in a longbow build by firing off crits like a machine gun and building a big stack of evade, or it could work in a serrated axe build to load a big stack of bleed on the enemy. In other words, your choice of starter attacks isn't just deck bloat that you'll get rid of--it affects how your build works (although you can also dump them entirely and use cards that don't have the "basic attack" mechanic on them). Different mechanics can be combined to ramp off of each other. For example, there is an enchant that buffs your basic attacks by the amount of poison on the enemy, so you can build a huge stack of poison and shred the enemy with massive attacks. Or the poison itself can be buffed to do more damage per tick in a pure poison build. The main point here is that due to the good game design, the number of possible builds is completely insane, and the runs are long enough that you have time to merge multiple builds together and get it to work. The detractors seemingly fall into a two camps. One group is mad that they are getting wrecked and that they can't use meta-progression to brute force their way to wins. It's true that the game is challenging, and that there are plenty of enemies and bosses mid-run with mechanics that could be hard counters to certain builds in the same way as a typical Slay the Spire endboss. But there are plenty of tools to mitigate that if you know what's coming, and you also have your choice of three entirely different areas at every run chapter. It's basic common sense, like--if you're spamming dozens of bare-fisted strike cards per turn, maybe don't go to the poison swamp unless you have poison removal or can kill the enemies before they act. In other words: It's a roguelike. Dawncaster just happens to have a lot more content than other games so it takes longer to learn, but for me that's part of the fun. The other group dismisses it as a "cheap mobile port," which is obviously at tension with the first group. If it's just a crappy mobile game, why aren't they winning easily? Why aren't PC-native developers putting card pools of this size in their games? In other words, the origins of the game are irrelevant to whether it is actually good. There are also complaints about "mobile game grinding," but I find them inaccurate. The meta-progression is slow, but it mainly unlocks different weapons and playstyles. The boosts from unlocking things like a small health bonus are very marginal and not needed to have a good run. But there is a reflex among some gamers to see a big unlock tree and think they need to "grind" to win when the size of the tree is just reflective of the massive amount of content and the real problem is a "skill issue." Bottom Line: It would be wrong to conclude that Dawncaster is a mediocre game from the mixed reviews, as 7/10 deckbuilders are a dime-a-dozen. But Dawncaster is something different and much less common--a great game that is highly polarizing. Depending on which group you fall in, you will either hate it or it will be one of your favorite games.

《Dawncaster》是一款由故事驱动的卡牌肉鸽游戏，一开始幻视《月圆之夜》了，但是随着游玩进程的推进，逐渐发现其上头之处…… 首先一般的卡牌肉鸽游戏基本都只有有限的“主体组合”，如《杀戮尖塔》中有四个角色，除了一些等级提升来解锁卡牌，其他成长都需要在游戏内获取，但是本作就大不一样了，本作的组合可以说是丰富到夸张。 6种职业，均有不同的形象展示，每种职业都有10种武器，特性对应适配的牌组，拿奥术师举例，有连续攻击增伤的雷击玩法，还有火焰冰冻玩法等，更夸张的是，制作组似乎对10这个数有什么执念，武器之后还有10种初始天赋、10张初始卡牌，稍微排列组合一下就能知道游戏光组合就能达到六千种，更别提还有完全随机的玩法。 游戏中组合甚多，想要短时间深入游玩显然是不可能的，于是我就暂且挑了一种最基础的玩法——奥术师的雷击玩法，本作能看到许多卡牌游戏的影子，比如说《炉石传说》《杀戮尖塔》以及模式最类似的《月圆之夜》。 本作以故事驱动，每场开局似乎都是完全随机的，随机的事件，随机的地图，同一个角色游玩也会有完全不同的体验。有时你可能开局会护送商队通行，有时你可能遇到一个耐心的老师，游戏的随机性可称形散神聚，肉鸽的魅力可见一斑。 回归前文，奥术师的雷击玩法是什么体验，这就不得不提到特殊词条了，“连锁”这一词条，就是你每次出带本词条的牌时都会增加伤害，相当于别的游戏中的“连击”，职业要强大起来就应该专注于一种套路，是火法就专挑燃烧，是冰法就专挑冻结，卡组的庞大也能够支持这一行为。 不过本作亦有缺陷，首先就是翻译的问题，大部分文案都比较正常，但是偶尔有的选择就变成纯英文了，还有就是容错率不高，玩到第二关boss的时候直接展现出跟第二层其他怪物完全不一样的强度，一套直接给我秒了，当然不排除是我卡组不够完善的缘故。 总体来说本作是一款能边看故事边体会卡牌肉鸽魅力的游戏，值得一试。 [quote] 闲暇时光，不妨试试游戏。 欢迎关注[url=store.steampowered.com/curator/45653622/] 闲暇時光鉴赏组 [/url] [/quote]
Bad balance
每种职业都有几套天赋，武器，组合，卡牌总类也巨多，还有各种乱入怪，设定很好，就是TM赚金币巨慢，解锁其他天赋太难了，20小时全部金币砸在一个职业才解60%你敢信?强烈建议翻3倍,新手也容易玩进去，最后说说翻译，还有待完善，一些卡牌意思很有深度，确实不好翻译和理解。

Meta progression is excessively slow, events and interactions require memorization with no assistance (you either know what it does or you don't and you can ruin your whole run on it because the consequences are not explained ahead of time), the storylines are almost childishly simplistic (not worth engaging with), clicking to move ahead in dialogue often double clicks (good thing talking to people doesn't really matter...until it does), the dialogue selection moves up or down with the character portrait so you can click on the portrait once and then accidentally double click dialogue that appears under your cursor (very cool), the mana choice option is still tilting left or right (its a computer, open a prompt), and hovering over doesn't open items to expand on them - you have to click on them which is something that most other games in the genre would penalize (clicking on a card takes the card, it doesn't expand it.) Oh but you can sync your mobile progression, meaning the two are linked so the PC progression is not going to be sped up as that would ruin the mobile game progression which is...certainly a choice (a bad one.) The games core concept is solid, the deckbuilding is fine, and overall I want to be more positive but when I saw a Dawncaster PC port I was definitely not expecting them to keep the worst part - the horrible HORRIBLY SLOW meta progression and the excessive, pointless, dialogue options with characters that have cardboard depth (there's a nice skip button sometimes, capitulating to how pointless it is.) The progression has to be accelerated and changed and if that means decoupling it from mobile, please do so immediately. Also mod support because clearly QOL stuff like knowing whether or not I'm going to waste my visit to an NPC because I can't afford their services without keeping a wiki open in another tab isn't going to come from the developers.
游戏内容还可以，就是单局游戏时间有点略长，如果能出个单局短一点的模式就好了。 - 目前最致命的缺点是汉化，汉化文本部分地方缺失，比如卡包的词条概述就没汉化，加上选卡包的时候也不能点进去查看100多张卡具体是啥，导致目前开局选启用哪些扩展卡包的时候不太方便。 - 综合还是不错的游戏，在汉化优化后值得一试。
Excellent deckbuilder, it maybe better than Slay the Spire. Can't recommend enough.

I’ve played 16 hours in two days and am frantically pounding this review out so I can get back to my run. Dawncaster is a relatively chunky roguelite deckbuilder with meta progression. The closest comparison I can give you in terms of presentation and mechanics is Vault of the Void, which I thoroughly enjoyed as well. Dawncaster is also not a new game in that it has been available on mobile for what seems to be quite a while, given that the Steam release gives you several expansions into the bargain on top of the base game. The game made me chuckle a bit when the first thing that appeared when I loaded it up was a developer news message basically saying “Guys! We promise we haven’t half-assed the mobile port, this game actually works on your PC!”. And yes, credit where it’s due I guess, if they hadn’t self-reported that this was a mobile port I probably wouldn’t have noticed – the UI is perfectly serviceable, with only one very minor visual bug in 16 hours that a quick restart solved. In terms of mechanics, Dawncaster doesn’t do anything you haven’t seen before, but it does lots of things quite well. You play cards, deal damage, gain buffs, inflict debuffs, equip items, all the good jazz. There is a multicoloured energy system that plays a tactical role for certain character classes, and most of the classic deck building/tweaking/polishing contrivances you know and love are in this game. The core strength of Dawncaster is the staggering array of deckbuilding choices available to you, even without activating any of the expansions. There are 6-7 initial character classes, all with their own paella of esoteric mechanics that your brain will slurp up greedily. Like all stupid idiots, after playing the 12 second tutorial and finishing my first run I immediately clicked new game and proceeded to activate all of the expansions and set every setting to random because I’m a god gamer. I have lost every single run since doing this, but I don’t care what the universe says, I’m a god gamer and all the buttons are staying on green thank you. There is a test you can do to see if this game is something you want to buy. Read this sentence: “Cascade. Chain 2. Deal X damage, where X is your Ephemeral stacks. If you are in Red Dawn Stance, Prognosticate twice, reducing the cost of both cards Prognosticated by 1 Green Energy.” If your brain just ejaculated all over the inside of your skull, congratulations this game is now in your basket, have fun. A run in Dawncaster (assuming you don’t die) is really quite long in comparison to other games of this genre. You fight dozens of enemies in one, and depending on your build, each fight can take several minutes. One benefit of this is that you are given plenty of time to discover, theorycraft, refine and ultimately perfect your deck, through card removal, upgrades and other shenanigans. But the flip side is that, in tandem with the game’s complexity, runs can be very mentally draining, running into 2-3 hours if your deck is a slow burner. And you cannot afford to autopilot in this game either, mindlessly playing the same sequence of cards until the You Win noises play. Many enemies have abilities and passive effects that can annihilate your deck’s synergy with but a wave of their demonic claw unless you are paying close attention to what they are doing versus what you are doing. This is great from a tactical perspective, but I have found myself shouting “How many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemies ARE THERE?” at the screen more than once. The game has done a decent job with the story you follow in each run. There are actual NPCs in this game, some of which simply provide you with the heroic motivation to journey forth, others providing benefits to you and your precious deck. There is this quite cute little detail in that once you’ve heard all the dialogue before in previous run, there is a “skip” dialogue option that says something like “Yeah yeah yeah I know just give me the damn quest already” and the NPCs actually react like you said that, saying “Oh, excuse me then, I’ll just go away shall I?”. It’s a nice touch that shows a bit of effort, and I appreciate that in any game. I also find the music in this game surprisingly ear-perking at times. I’ve noticed some reviews displeased with the slow speed of the meta-progression in Dawncaster. You definitely do get a sense for this when you start playing – as I mentioned, runs are long and often gruelling endeavours, and even when you win, the currency you receive is unlikely to net you more than 3 or 4 unlocks for one of the many character classes (to clarify, all characters are available from start, it’s things like their starting weapon and ability). It is a little stingy, but at the same time, there is so much choice available to you in terms of card choices and the expansions, I don’t think it’s fair to lambast the project for this. If you’re an “I want everything now now now” type player, I doubt you’re going to enjoy a deckbuilder with runs that can last over 3 hours anyway. Some criticisms. The game teases you with a card upgrade system, but I guarantee the disappointment will hit you hard when you realise that in this game, you can only really upgrade damage dealing cards (usually the least interesting). In a genre that has so many competitors offering bespoke upgrading systems for every single card in their game, playing Dawncaster is an absolute tease in this regard. To be fair, there are HUNDREDS of different cards in this game, all with whacked out mechanics and keywords, but it still hurts to not be able to upgrade Quantum Euclidean Apotheosis so it also gives me six stacks of Waffly Bunt Mastery every turn or whatever. Sigh. Another quibble is information. When you select any card, any keywords or other points of note appear in tooltip explanations in the top left of the screen. Well, most of the time they do. Sometimes they don’t, and the only way to find out is to either Google it (which god gamers do not do) or just take the damn thing and play it and see if you die. Most of the time you don’t die, which is good, but also most of the time you’ll be chucking it out of your deck at the very next campfire you encounter. Another personal quibble – the encounters. During a run you will experience “random” events. However, once you know the outcome of each choice through trial and error, these events become little more than rote clicking exercises. I know other games do this, but for some reason it just irks me. But let’s circle back to the positives. This game, in my opinion, makes an outstanding first impression. And it achieves the holy grail of all deckbuilders, which is this: you start a new run, and when you kill your first enemy, it offers you a choice of cards to add to your deck. Your eyes scan the smorgasbord before you, but then one card draws your gaze. It has a keyword, maybe two. The artwork looks cool. And your imagination takes over – what other cards might support this one? What existing cards in your deck would support it? How dirty is it in bed? You pick it, and you feel the game whispering “ooooh good choice”. And then you’re off to the races. God, is that the time? I could have done another run instead of this nonsense!

[b]Edit:[/b] Yes, I continued to play. I played a lot. But the reasons are not it's a 'good game'. One, I was in a period where my job wasn't very demanding, and this was one of the games I could play on my garbage laptop Two, and more importantly, I'm probably autistic, and I hate when a card game 'beats' me. So, I went back and played. I beat Impossible difficulty with every class (check my achievements if you like). Yeah, there's some cool stuff here; I never meant to say there wasn't anything to like. But, ultimately, I still think this game is inferior to the greats of the genre. If you've played and beaten all the better games, this one isn't bad. But if it's this OR something better - and there are many in this latter category - don't get this. Finally, the meta-progession is an absolute crime. I mastered the game, to the extent that I was building original decks to beat Impossible difficulty [b]with the hard paths[/b] and I still wouldn't have had all the unlocks for more than one character. That alone is enough to dock it. If you do buy this game, I uploaded a 30-second guide to skip the unlocks. [hr][/hr] Initially, I really enjoyed this. There a ton of cards and synergies and different ways to build your character: it's very deep. So why the thumb's down? Well, I am a veteran of these games. I have hundreds, perhaps a thousand, hours across Monster Train, Slay the Spire, Vault of the Void, Balatro. I mean, I have like twenty hours in Dog Witch. What makes those games good is that you have a high degree of agency: if you fail, at least the vast majority of the time, there was something you could have done better. Yes, draws are random. Yes, the card pool available to you is semi-random. But, the designers incorporate mechanics to help you mitigate this. It's why even in a game as punishing as StS, for example, the best players can have win-streaks even at the highest difficulty. Deckbuilders are, at their core, about improving your skills and knowledge. The designers of this game, however, didn't seem to appreciate that lesson. There are several mechanics in the game that completely strip your agency. There are several debuffs that prevent you from making meaningful decisions and are often applied on turn 1 due to 'first-strike', [b]there is no counter-play[/b]. One example literally forces you to play cards in a random order. So even if you: knew the debuff was coming, had a card in your deck to counter it, [i]and[/i] drew it on turn one, you [b]still[/b] can't play it unless the effect selects that card to be playable. And several important enemies re-apply that debuff every. single. turn. There are plenty of examples: [list] [*] Enemies that destroy random cards on turn one, potentially ruining a combo deck [*] Enemies that prevent you from gaining armour throughout the entire fight and into the next [*] Enemies that replace cards in your deck. [*] Enemies that dispel or steal your barrier, with no protection - at least none that I could find [/list] I understand that some of these things are present in other deckbuilders; I really do. But they are so egregious and so prevalent in this game that it becomes deeply frustrating. And allowing enemies to apply these effects before you get any chance to act is a violation of one of the fundamental rules of good deckbuilders: the player should always have a [i]chance[/i] to do something. There's a lot of style to the game, and it's certainly not all bad. And, hey, for twenty bucks I got twenty hours of play. But if you're trying to decide between this game and another deckbuilder, I wouldn't recommend this one. Oh, also, the progression to new weapons and portraits and stuff is [i]glacial[/i]. If you want to skip all that, just edit the file 'DC_Conf.dc' in C:\Users\<user>\AppData\LocalLow\Wanderlost Interactive\Dawncaster. There's a value called "m_CurrentFateShards", just set that to whatever you want.

I do not see that as at all likely here and it's a pity. They have clearly put a lot of work into balance here... but that can turn into a tiresome cage for developer and player alike.

(Note: I play Dawncaster mainly on my mobile device, my Steam play hours do not accurately reflect my play time) Dawncaster is my new obsession. I have played games such as Hearthstone and MTG in the past, and those are great games. And then came Slay the Spire, which opened up a new style of battler games for me. And then I found Dawncaster and I can't seem to stop playing it. The game is incredibly well balanced while also remaining broad-based. There is no "one OP build", you can make any build work, and the approaches to this feel endless, from character choices to card synergy and beyond. You can choose a freeze/burn build, or learn to bury cards, or trim your deck, or raise massive stats, or gain souls, pickup companions, trade-up for ultra powerful cards, gain experience, choose difference paths, use buffs/debuffs, and so on. The sheer number of builds, approaches and some luck is overwhelming and offers endless gameplay. Once you think you have a build that works for you, up the difficulty and find your flaws! This games comes with all the cards already so you won't be nagged endlessly for DLC's, and you can easily earn gold in game for assets that you want. I've never spent a dime past my initial purchase price which was already very reasonable. As mentioned, Dawncaster is also available on Android, (although the cloud saves don't align with PC). This is just nice as it doesn't matter which platform I'm on, I can always play Dawncaster. If you play and like the game, I encourage you to learn more about it. There is a lot of stuff to learn that isn't obvious at first, such as how to choose which energy to use when playing a card, how to choose which paths to follow, all the extra asset packs that aren't normally in play, and the endless combinations of new builds those assets packs include. Try different approaches, learn new ways to take the enemy down. I went from failing to reach the end of the game the first few times to making my first run where I didn't need a single rest to heal, and it felt great! The more you try, the more fun it is!
It might be worthwhile to add the option to save your run after completing a boss. Starting ALL the way over from the beginning of the game each time is frustrating, and a weakness of the genre.

各位百官，列位诸公。 希望在你购买或者参考其他人的评论之前，可以稍微花点时间看完这条评测，或许能够帮到你。 Q：这游戏好玩吗？ A：是否好玩是一个主观评价。 我的评价是：很好玩的肉鸽卡牌，还支持多端云同步（可能需要魔法）。 Q：你的时长毫无说服力。 A：因为我主要在手机上玩，前几年和现在都是。 Q：全是机翻？ A：不完全是，部分卡牌效果和词条是经过人工修订的。 Q：为何如此？ A：因为游戏的多语言翻译（特别是中文）的基底就是机翻，高度依赖玩家的反馈来进行修订。 Q：哪些是人工修订的？ A：大家对部分显而易见的卡牌效果以及词条的错误进行了修订和润色，但任重而道远。 Q：怎么翻译后的效果是错误的？ A：版本更新了/译本更新滞后/我忘了改/我改迷糊了/不是我改的 Q：怎么翻译不通顺/风格不统一？ A：没有人来负责整个项目的统筹与推进。我所认识的译者都只是利用闲暇之余对机翻进行修修补补的普通发电玩家。 Q：有多少人在参与？ A：这是一个开放的项目，欢迎所有人来参加。所以，我不清楚。 Q：目前在翻译哪个部分？ A：在努力把所有卡牌和词条修订到大家都能看懂。至于对话？祝我长寿。 Q：什么时候能完成汉化？ A：没法统计。我们也要为自己的生计奔波。 Q：我能啃生肉吗？ A：如果你的英语达到四级，你就已经能看懂绝大部分卡牌的文本内容了，剩下的小部分生僻词可以通过截图翻译来理解。 Q：我没过四级怎么办？ A：展现游戏经验和理解的时候到了，剩下的用勇气去补足！ Q：我有更好的翻译建议/我想参与汉化，该如何提交？ A：你可以在这篇评测下面留言，或者前往官方DC频道。 Q：太棒了，我逐渐理解一切。 A：那可以给我点个赞让更多人看到这条评测吗？谢谢！

NB: I don't really like deckbuilders like Slay the Spire. I play stuff like Path of Exile because I like the loot, buildcrafting, and power-scaling. Dialogue, events etc are all the same each time so I use the game's official reference site "Blightbane" to look up event outcomes and card lists to help with making my deck builds. $20 gets you the base game + all 5 expansions on PC, but **you can get just the base game on mobile for $2** with none of the expansions; The base game is so good that I think either way is a good deal. I'd guess there's probably 100+ hours of different builds in this game. PROS: + Tons of build variety & content + Strong themes; Thief feels completely different than Warrior, and Bow-Thief has a totally different gameplay style compared to Dagger-Thief or Bomb-Thief. + You can really draft a concise, strong deck consistently. Card removal is plentiful and cheap. + (I think) Runs are deterministic. Certain paths will result in the same outcomes but in different orders, like finding a cost-reduction upgrade shrine in the second zone or a boss always dropping a certain legendary artifact to add to your deck. Game knowledge is rewarded CONS: - Enemies can brick runs; Game knowledge is rewarded, but new players & blindly playing can be punishing. - Expansions massively dilute the card discovery pool; New players should probably only enable whatever expansions enable your desired build, starting with just the Core cards w/o any expansions at all.

After 13 hours with Dawncaster, I’m really impressed. The art is beautiful, the atmosphere is strong, and the card synergies are the kind that make you keep saying “just one more run.” I spent most of my first dozen hours playing Hunter and had a great time learning how the class works. The game gives you a lot of starting choices, and those choices actually matter. Different weapons, talents, shrines, opportunities, and card rewards can push a run in completely different directions. When a build comes together, it feels fantastic. What I like most is that Dawncaster has real depth without feeling overwhelming. There are plenty of keywords and mechanics to learn and the game rewards experimenting. You start noticing little connections between cards, talents, and events, and suddenly a deck that looked simple turns into a powerful engine. The art deserves special mention. The cards, enemies, and locations all have a distinct style that makes the world feel dark, strange, and memorable. If you enjoy deckbuilders with strong build variety, meaningful choices, and satisfying synergies, Dawncaster is easy to recommend.

An ultimately disappointing adventure. I was initially excited to see it had cross save on the phone, so I purchased it on android and then PC, only to find out that it only saved your meta progression, not your current run... which were way to long and the point of cross saving. Not only are the runs long and boring (because your card pool and strategy rarely change) but the meta progression equates to 10 extra life, or some cosmetic portrait each level. The game bragged about having a massive card pool, which it does, but none of the cards synergize outside of it's own mechanic. Because you aren't forced to take a card each round, your deck ends up being the same as there's no reason to take any card outside your niche. Boss fights CAN be interesting, but most of the time it's just a crap shoot trying to leverage your mechanic against whatever special conditions they have. Also the "RPGadventure" aspect isn't any different than any other game that I could tell. You're presented with the same "choices" with different buff/debuff outcomes that all the other cardgames basically present. The overarching story isn't that spectacular, though I haven't played any of the expansions. Some of the deck mechanics were neat to play, but my time with it ultimately didn't feel rewarding. Originally I wanted a casual card slinger to kill time while I gave Breach Wanderers a break. However, in most every aspect, this game disappointed me and I'll gladly sink more time into the aforementioned.

I'm a veteran in these kinds of games and this one feels like I'm playing a slot machine with little player agency. Because of the huge card set with almost no synergy between the expansions, getting a combo or cards that work well together is rare. So the consequence is in combat, especially the first biomes, you repetitively play the exact same combo about 1000 times, and only the visual representation of the enemy image changes... (you never fight more than 1 enemy). Doesn't matter what the enemy does, you have no choice but to play your 1 combo, or closest thing you have to a combo, 1000s of times. Furthermore, you repetitively prioritize the same events, of deleting your same useless cards for the same combo which is decided by your starting set. I feel like I should get an AI to go through the motions for me until later game. Therefore, I am basically prompted to think only when and if the slot machine proposes a card that is synergetic for deckbuilding, which is a very rare event, and otherwise I find myself mindlessly clicking like a machine 1000 times, prioritizing the starting set. I'm quite surprised that if the game has been out for this long, and if card diversity is the selling point of this game, that the devs haven't done the minimal work to get sets of expansions for a character to have synergy, instead of being mostly antagonistic. I'll think about it, but I'm probably going to refund. Also with newer deckbuilders, or autobattlers, they are increasing strategical planning with other elements like city building, economy etc., but this game feels like it's taking steps back... and especially the important ones. So I'll probably look to the future of this genre. EDIT/Update: So I decided I'll finish the game. I beat it on challenging difficulty after about 12 hours of play time, I'll work on the last levels of difficulty. I confirm that I basically just spammed 1 combo (didn't have much choice to create others), except on about 2 monsters that had ridiculously cheesy mechanics. Mostly felt like slot machine luck in order to obtain the necessary talents/cards to beat the game. Since this game has been around a long time, there is a decent amount of content, but it feels more like quantity than quality, especially because it was confined to mobile all these prior years. Verdict: I prefer the PC game big hit alternatives, like Knock on the Coffin Lid, STS I/II, Vault of the Void, and Monster Train I/II, they offer better feel, more strategical dimensions, snappier reactivity (here in Dawncaster, god awful bell sound every round starts without possibility of muting or replacing it, and slower playing cards waiting for turns to finish). Dawncaster seems like a good choice if you plan playing on mobile/tablet, where you only want to think halfway while doing something else, if you want simpler, or if you're obsessed with deckbuilders and you've already completed the major ones.

Doesn't quite scratch the same itch as Slay The Spire to be honest. The "RPG story" aspect of it is interesting at first but then since you're still playing a roguelike, you end up optimizing away the intrigue to focus on what the outcomes of decisions instead. Upgrading your cards is so incremental that it's really uninteresting unless you have talents that allow you to upgrade repeatedly. Cards don't really seem to synergize with each other across different sets so having more cards in the pool doesn't really help with build variety and usually does the opposite in which you use your bonus re-rolls to funnel yourself into very set-isolated decks. Aside from this I am not a fan of the responsiveness of the UI, weird little quirks that don't seem as polished as other games. Interesting ideas, but the execution doesn't quite hit right.

[h1][b]5.5/10[/b][/h1] TL;DR: RNG So torn on this one. It could have been absolutely stellar with some more effort. I was hoping for an experience more like Hex: Shards of Fate or Etherlords II or something (a single player deck building experience). It's slightly like that, but the entire thing is poisoned by being more like Slay the Spire. Still moderately fun though. 4.2/5 Great card neo-roguelike (advancement through loss) game. Modern graphics, decent mechanism, interesting DLCs (get all of them). Some interesting and complicated worm holes. Slightly fuzzy on a bunch of things which degrade from the score. For example, when going up a level there's no way to review one's character sheet. This means when one is choosing the most important upgrades in the game, you can't look at your current stats, "talents", etc. Very annoying. Also, the game has a bunch of bugs, though infrequent. The major bug is that after winning a battle, the reward screen blurs the background and no options appear. Most likely to occur when going up a level, which makes it very annoying. Also more likely if one has just beaten a boss. On the very plus side, quitting the game in that frozen-blur state, one can re-play the fight again and .. sometimes? ... the error doesn't occur. But if it does re-occur, around 90% of the time, the best work around is to do ANYTHING you can think of to try to change the seed. Solutions include simply opening the card list, resorting. But the best way to avoid the bug is any "real" choice in the game. A different monster, a camp, an opportunity, whatever. But this is a super annoying bug if one is trying to thread the needle on the game's most complicated and difficult paths. If the bug occurs while you're on one of the advanced 'secret' tracks (see sun tree twig), hours and hours of play can be completely lost to a stupid bug. recommended. Interesting and boring in just the right level. I'd give this a 4.5/5 if the horrible buggy problem didn't waste my time. [as always with all my reviews, Steam is mis-reporting my play time because i leave the game running when I close my laptop and Steam continues to count "hours of play" even if I haven't touched the game in days. I think I've played about 200 hours, Steam says 1100 hours.]
